title: A branch with no shared history, in the same repository
summary: Documentation sites, generated artefacts and legal archives sometimes need to live in the repository without polluting the code history. An orphan branch is a second root — same repository, separate history.
mental_model: `switch --orphan` gives you a branch whose first commit will have no parent. It shares the object database with everything else, but reaches none of it — the same mechanism behind a `gh-pages` branch.

setup.run: git commit -q -m "Add app and documentation source"

steps.title: Build the site from the source
steps.why: The generated HTML is derived output. Committing it to main would mean every documentation change produces two commits and a diff nobody reads.
steps.expect: A built site/ directory, currently untracked.

steps.title: Create the orphan branch
steps.why: `switch --orphan` moves HEAD to a branch that does not exist yet and stages nothing from the current commit. The index is emptied — that clearing is what makes the next commit a root.
steps.expect: On gh-pages with no commits, and the working tree still holding your files as untracked.

verify.label: you are on the orphan branch (rev-parse cannot resolve HEAD until it has a commit)

steps.title: Commit only the built output
steps.why: Add just the site's files, so the branch contains the published artefact and nothing else. This is what a documentation host serves, and why it must not carry your source tree.
steps.expect: One commit, one file, and NO parent line in the commit object.

verify.label: the branch contains only the published artefact
its first commit is a root — no parent

steps.title: Confirm the two histories never meet
steps.why: `merge-base` returns nothing, and `git log --all --graph` shows two disconnected trees. That separation is the feature: a documentation rebuild can never conflict with a code change.
steps.expect: No merge base, and two root commits.

verify.label: the repository now has two independent roots

steps.title: Go back and see the branches are unrelated
steps.why: main is untouched and has never heard of the site. Switching between them replaces the working tree wholesale, because they share no files at all.
steps.expect: Your source tree back, with no index.html and no site commits in the log.

verify.label: main never received the built artefact

steps.title: Publish updates without switching branches
steps.why: A worktree is the right tool here: check the orphan branch out into its own directory and the publish step becomes a build plus a commit, with no branch switching in your main checkout at all.

pitfalls: `git switch --orphan` leaves your previous branch's files in the working tree as untracked. Add only what belongs on the orphan branch, or you will commit the whole source tree onto it.
The older spelling is `git checkout --orphan`, which does NOT clear the index — you must `git rm -rf .` yourself. The `switch` form is safer.
Merging an orphan branch into main needs `--allow-unrelated-histories` and is almost always a mistake. They are meant to stay apart.
Rebuilding a generated site on every commit makes the orphan branch's history enormous. Some teams force-push a single commit to it instead, deliberately discarding its history.
Use a worktree rather than switching branches to publish. Switching wipes your working tree and any running build.
cheatsheet: start a branch with no history
empty means the branches are unrelated
publish it like any other branch
